title: thought process of biotech startup ideas
tldr: a) what customers want b) how building that thing will fit into a larger mission c) and what is just now possible d) what you are interested in.
text:
i actually dont like that phrasing but for the purpose of letting people know what I'm writing about, that's what I chose. I like the framing of finding a problem in biotech that I care about so much that I'm willing to suffer for it. 

anyway, Maxx Young ((https://www.maxxyung.com/)) is one step ahead of me on my journey so looking at his blog serves as a good place for me to follow his playbook. so here is the playbook to starting a biotech company from 0:

"Following this framework, Phase 0 of most hardtech companies should follow this rough timeline:

Month 1: Secure initial capital (usually from family & friends) to begin.
Month 2-3: Prototype the tech, innovating on just a few core aspects.
Month 4: Demonstrate the MVP and a path to commercialization through LOIs.
Months 5-6: Begin fundraising your seed round for the development of V2."  
((https://brain.maxxyung.com/blog/venture/hardtech-beginnings))

okay that is great, but to prototype the tech,  i need to know what i am building. and I'm sort of at this point of tension where I feel like I should just be building right now, but also not want to waste my time building something that I'm going to pivot away from in an orthogonal direction so for a deep tech company, I want to give sufficient thought to the idea, even though this seems to be against the Silicon Valley ethos. 

okay, so i need an idea. In his blog about ideation (( https://brain.maxxyung.com/blog/venture/thesis )), he points out a good idea: you should aim to do stuff that is only now possible. And I think there are a few things to note here. here is my thought process: 

- Foundation Model Labs are a new customer. They will buy data that will train their models. I'm interested in the biological lane. And I think there is a super interesting stack going on from how granular the level of data being collected is: 
    - behavioral data 
    - collecting biological multi omics data. and since i know a little more about this ill note: and there is more to indicate about like emphasis on different omics data collection ie one company may go like more balls deep on like transcript level vs idk further from the dna like emphasis on protein data. i think this comes down to understanding the trajectory of sequencing tech and talking to customers
        - and on collecting bio data, there is opportunity for further differentiation by the model that you pick. 
    - collecting chemical readouts of a biological process
    - collecting physics readouts of a biological process
    - ((is the answer to go vertical in this sense? maybe as a you develop but starting off with what the customers want is prob best and expanding past there))

And then you return back to the question as to what is just now possible that frontier AI labs and big pharma companies want (presuming these are your customers) but no one has done yet. This involves talking to our customers and perhaps developing a thesis then. 

((https://www.vivodyne.com/ and contellationlab.io and https://www.engram.co/ is somewhere in that stack))

More notable points about things to take into consideration are what is just now possible: 
- There have been advances in robotics for automated research. 
So now you have automated research that will make data for a new customer class. 
- But this just seems to be a saturated area. Not to say that you can't build on it. It's more like you have to come up with a complementary way of generating data, as opposed to just copying what someone else is doing ie finding your unique point in the vertical stack, as mentioned above. ((Peter Thiel on competition is for losers.))


In conclusion, given my interest in biotech, I'm inclined to build in a parallel data generation lane to other companies doing the same thing. 

But I think the important thing to note is that this is a practical plan to finance some large mission (i.e., it's a means to an end). 

what is my larger mission? This is what you rally people behind, what you're kind of about, and what you're going to suffer for. 

And like to answer this question, I think you have to consider the multi-dimensional environment about finding an equilibrium between a) what customers want b) how building that thing will fit into a larger mission c) and what is just now possible d) what you are interested in. 

((I also think a lot of this is top of the bell curve trying to figure out what to work on but still useful to think through. i should write about the importance of being a part of every part of the bell curve as opposed to jumping straight to the end ))
